extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, critics, and educated readers of dramatic poetry (esp. 17th-century English theatre)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and evaluative criteria for dramatic poetry and plays: language, wit, plotting, character, and suitability to contemporary conversation and audience. Focuses on what constitutes refinement or decay in dramatic writing and how to improve or judge it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement of Wit, Language, and Conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement of our Wit, Language and Conversation; or, an alteration in them for the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refinement comprises either rejecting ill-sounding or improper old words/phrases or admitting new words that are more proper, sounding, and significant. The essay treats refinement as measurable by clearer speech, fewer solecisms, and better-suited expressions for the age; it connects literary refinement to broader social conversation and courtly manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting Improper or Ill-sounding Antiquated Words/Phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement includes 'rejecting such old words, or phrases, which are ill sounding, or improper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rejection is praiseworthy only when the old words are improper (not merely archaic). The point is to excise solecisms and improper constructions rather than to reject antiquity for its age alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admitting New Words That Improve the Tongue
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement includes 'admitting new, which are more proper, more sounding, and more significant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New words can enrich the language (like bullion importation). Some admissions are necessary, others ornamental; follow Horace's rule—do not be too hasty in accepting neologisms but let custom familiarise them. Examples: many French phrases were adopted; some are useful, others mere fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Corrupting the Native Idiom by Excessive Foreign (French) Mixing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not corrupt English idiom by mixing it too much with French; that is a sophistication, not an improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fops who transplant French phrases without need are prescribing fashions, not words. Borrow only when necessary or superior; prefer native expressions when equal or better. The essay condemns those who 'turn English into French' unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Received Words to New Significations (Inventive Usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement by applying received words to a new signification (Horace's precept: make a known word new by clever junction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grafting or innovation of sense beautifies the tongue (examples: Horace's felicitous tropes). Poets should heighten words' natural signification to craft fresh expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness of Language: Syntax, Grammar, and Elimination of Solecisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays and poems should avoid solecisms of speech and notorious flaws in sense; correctness of language is a mark of refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of anti-patterns: misplaced prepositions at line ends, redundant pronouns ('they' redundant), false agreement ('ones' plural), wrong articles ('his wrath' for heaven), antiquated or wrong words ('be' for 'are'). Observing and correcting such errors is an important improvement over earlier ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-placing of Words and Sweetness of Pronunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sweetness of pronunciation through well-placing of words is an aesthetic criterion introduced by later writers (e.g., Mr Waller).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions that break the flow or place prepositions and conjunctions inconveniently; favor word-order that enhances sound and ease of utterance. The essay cites examples of syncopated or ill-placed constructions as faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Obscurity, Bombast, and Incomprehensible Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines or speeches that are bombastic, perplexed, or 'not to be understood' are faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ben Jonson's comment on some Macbeth speeches as 'horror' is used to illustrate bombast. Ensure clarity and intelligibility; avoid inflated language that obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Diction by Genre (High Diction for Tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy ought to be 'more high and sounding' than other kinds of poetry; diction should suit the genre's dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid meanness of expression in tragedy; choose elevated language and maintain it consistently throughout works appropriate to their genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct Plotting, Coherence, and Decorum of the Stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic plots should be well-constructed, coherent, and observe the decorum of the stage; poorly made, incoherent, or impossible plots are faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticises lameness in earlier plots (e.g., Pericles, Winter's Tale) and Fletcher's occasional inability to 'understand correct plotting' or 'the decorum of the stage.' The essay recommends unified, plausible story development, avoiding ridiculous incoherence that occupies 'the business of an age.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of Matter and Judgment in Subject-Matter (Avoid Redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should exercise judgment and not indulge in redundancy or over-pleasure in matter; excess undermines effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fletcher criticized for 'redundancy of his matter' and failing to know when to stop; good writing requires discipline—avoid slumping in later acts from excessive initial material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of Tone and Suitability of Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistency of wit and tone appropriate to subject and character; avoid precipitous falls from high thought to low expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare exemplified both heights and lapses ('Janus of poets' — two faces). The writer should avoid fluctuating from lofty conception to base expression within or between scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: Naturalness, Class-appropriateness, and Avoidance of Mean Clownishness
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be fitting, well-chosen, and maintained to the end; humour should represent folly without mean or clownish offensiveness to refined audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jonson praised for choice of characters and maintenance; but his meanness of persons (tankard, rags) may be unsuitable for a polite audience. Comedy in a more civil age should present the follies of gentlemen (gentlemanly raillery), not merely vulgar clowning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Conversation and Contemporary Manners to Enrich Drama
rubrics_metrics.description: The refinement of conversation (courtly manners, gallantry) supplies material for better comedies; modern poets benefit by imitating present social discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden ascribes improvement to courtly influence and the king's example—poets should draw on current manners and conversation to render scenes lively and fitting to their audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-awareness: Addressing the Right Audience and its Capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic poets must attend to the nature of their audience (low crowd vs. courtly patrons), adjusting art, complexity, and appeals accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shakespeare wrote for varied public playhouses and thus used bold, original strokes to rouse broad audiences; Dryden wrote for a courtly audience of judges of composition and therefore emphasized art and critical knowledge. Consider venue and audience taste in style and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical Self-scrutiny and the Value of Severe Criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A severe critic helps a poet by restraining luxuriant fancy and pointing out faults; observation of errors is a step to correcting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay values critics for keeping writers within bounds; being able to observe one's own errors and those of predecessors is evidence of progress. This implies cultivating critical standards and being responsive to critique.
